packets.title: Intake pilot: 40 → 16 hours, and what the pilot did not measure

outline.heading: Intake pilot: 40 → 16 hours, and what the pilot did not measure
outline.goal: State the core message and the limitation up front so collaborators know what the deck does and does not establish.
outline.message: In this synthetic intake pilot, median review time was 40 hours before the pilot and 16 hours during it; review quality and error rates were not measured, so the time gain alone does not show a quality improvement.
outline.question: What is this deck about, and what is the one thing to take away?

outline.heading: Median review time fell from 40 hours before the pilot to 16 hours during it
outline.goal: Present the time result exactly as observed, as a before-versus-during contrast rather than an inferred effect size.
queries: median review time hours intake workflow
before after review time comparison pilot
outline.link: delivers the result the title promises
outline.message: Median review time was 40 hours before the pilot and 16 hours during the pilot [1]; the two figures are the median for the same pilot, reported as observation.
outline.question: How much faster was intake review during the pilot than before it?

outline.heading: The result rests on two teams over eight weeks of synthetic training data
outline.goal: Fix the scope of the observation and flag that the numbers are training data, not organizational results.
queries: two team pilot eight weeks duration
outline.link: narrows the result to its sample and data type
outline.message: The observation covered two teams over eight weeks, and the numbers are synthetic training data rather than actual organizational results [1].
outline.question: Where does the time result come from, and how far does it reach?

outline.heading: Review quality, error rates and other teams were not measured
outline.goal: Make the unmeasured dimensions explicit so they are not silently read into the time result.
queries: review quality and error rate measurement intake
outline.link: adds what the same pilot did not measure
outline.message: The two-team pilot did not measure review quality or error rates, and other teams were not evaluated [2].
outline.question: What did the pilot leave out?

outline.heading: A faster review cannot on its own establish a quality improvement
outline.goal: Show why the missing measures limit what the time result can support, which is the reason the decision needs them.
queries: speed versus quality trade-off in review
limits of before after pilot evidence
outline.link: draws the consequence of the unmeasured dimensions
outline.message: Observation: review time fell from 40 to 16 hours [1]. Interpretation limited by the pilot: because quality and error rates were not measured and other teams were not evaluated, faster review cannot establish better review [2].
outline.question: Why is the time result not enough to decide on?

outline.heading: Three options are on the table, none ranked and none costed
outline.goal: Close on the decision boundary: name the options, mark which evidence each would need, and label any recommendation as a proposal.
queries: decision options continue expand stop pilot
quality measure design for intake review
outline.link: turns the stated limitation into the decision on the table
outline.message: The note offers three unranked, uncosted options — continue measuring the two teams, expand with a quality measure, or stop the pilot [3]. Proposed action, not an evidence-based conclusion: any extension carries a quality and error-rate measure so the next decision rests on more than review time [2][3].
outline.question: What can collaborators decide now, and on what basis?

issues.problem: The heading "Median review time fell..." and the question "How much faster..." can imply a causal before/after effect, while C1 only reports medians before and during the pilot.
issues.fix: Use "was lower during the pilot (16 hours) than before (40 hours)" and avoid causal verbs; keep the comparison as an observation.

issues.problem: Slide 4 states "other teams were not evaluated," while C4's evidence says the sample does not establish an effect in other teams. The current wording is a stronger scope claim and drops the inferential limit.
issues.fix: Use the source wording: "the pilot does not establish an effect in other teams" or "other teams were not part of the pilot sample."

issues.problem: Slide 5 uses "other teams were not evaluated" as a reason that faster review cannot establish better review. C3 supports the quality conclusion, while C4 supports a separate generalization limit; the sentence merges them and leaves the generalization consequence implicit.
issues.fix: Separate the two inferences: quality/error-rate gap means the pilot cannot establish a quality improvement in the observed teams; other-team gap means the pilot does not establish an effect in other teams.

issues.problem: Slide 6 proposes that "any extension carries a quality and error-rate measure," which is broader than C5's three options and can merge "continue measuring the two teams" with "expand with a quality measure."
issues.fix: Keep the note's three options distinct and present the added measures as a separate recommendation, or attach them specifically to the expand option.

issues.problem: The page goal says to mark which evidence each option would need, but the message only names the options and one proposed measure.
issues.fix: Either add the evidence needed for each option or revise the goal so it matches the closing message.

packets.title: 两种阅读安排：分歧、证据与局限

outline.heading: 两种阅读安排：分歧、证据与局限
outline.goal: 让学生知道这份讲义讨论两种每周阅读安排，并先明确材料只记录了讨论意见。
outline.message: 这份合成课堂材料记录了对每周阅读安排的两种偏好：共同选书与自主选书。它反映讨论意见，没有测量阅读量或学习效果。
outline.question: 这份材料讨论什么，能回答到什么程度？

outline.heading: 分歧来自两个不同的课堂目标：共同讨论与照顾兴趣
outline.goal: 先说明分歧的来源，而不是直接评判哪种安排更好。
queries: 共同选书 讨论同一段落
自主选书 不同兴趣
阅读安排 目标 分歧
outline.link: 从核心问题进入分歧来源
outline.message: 记录显示，一组希望每周选择同一本书，以便讨论同一段落；另一组希望自主选书，以便照顾不同兴趣。两种主张的考虑点不同。
outline.question: 为什么会有两种阅读安排的主张？

outline.heading: 共同选书的理由是便于讨论同一段落，但记录没有效果证据
outline.goal: 区分共同选书主张的理由与材料能支持的范围。
queries: 学习效果 测量 阅读安排
outline.link: 先检查第一种主张的理由与证据边界
outline.message: 材料记录的理由是共同选书便于讨论同一段落，这属于讨论中的意见。记录没有测量阅读量或学习效果，因此不能据此判断共同选书更有效。
outline.question: 支持共同选书的证据是什么，局限在哪里？

outline.heading: 自主选书的理由是照顾不同兴趣，但同样缺少效果证据
outline.goal: 用与上一页相同的方式检查第二种主张，避免只审视一方。
outline.link: 接着用同样方式检查第二种主张
outline.message: 材料记录的理由是自主选书能照顾不同兴趣，这同样是讨论中的意见。记录没有测量阅读量或学习效果，因此也不能据此判断自主选书更有效。
outline.question: 支持自主选书的证据是什么，局限在哪里？

outline.heading: 记录只反映讨论意见：阅读量、学习效果和统一决定都未测量
outline.goal: 把两种主张放回共同局限，防止学生把偏好当成效果结论。
queries: 阅读量 学习效果 未测量
交替使用 阅读安排
outline.link: 两种主张都受同一限制，因此转向共同局限
outline.message: 参与者没有形成统一决定。两种安排可以在不同时段交替使用，但记录没有检验这种安排的效果；应保留分歧和未测量的限制。
outline.question: 哪些结论是材料不能支持的？

outline.heading: 先保留分歧，再把阅读安排当作需要检验的选择
outline.goal: 收束现有证据，并给出不超出材料的下一步。
queries: 阅读安排 效果 检验
outline.link: 从共同局限收束到可核查的下一步
outline.message: 现有材料只能说明两种偏好及其理由，不能说明哪种安排更有效。若要做出取舍，需要补充对阅读量和学习效果的测量，并检验包括交替使用在内的安排。
outline.question: 在现有证据下，应该怎样看待这两种阅读安排？

issues.problem: 结尾页提出「若要做出取舍，需要补充对阅读量和学习效果的测量，并检验包括交替使用在内的安排」。这是本讲义作者的建议，卡片1–4只记录讨论意见与未测量的限制，没有任何卡片提出过测量或检验方案。
issues.fix: 把这句话明确标注为「建议（非材料记录）」，或在页面上把它与「材料记录了什么」分栏呈现，避免学生把它读成材料结论。

issues.problem: 标题「分歧来自两个不同的课堂目标」和问题「为什么会有两种阅读安排的主张」把记录中的理由升级为分歧的成因解释；卡片1、2只记录了两组各自提出的理由，没有分析分歧的原因。
issues.fix: 改为「记录中的两种理由」这类表述，并在页面上注明这是对记录理由的归类，不是材料给出的成因分析。

issues.problem: 「记录没有测量阅读量或学习效果」这一限制在p1、p3、p4、p5四处重复陈述，p3与p4的推理结构完全相同，读起来像同一段话换主语。
issues.fix: p3、p4只用一句短提示指向共同限制，把完整陈述留给p5；两页各自保留不同的理由与不同的问题焦点。

issues.problem: 封面副标题已经给出「反映讨论意见，没有测量阅读量或学习效果」的总结，而简报要求先讲为什么会有分歧；封面提前给出结论性总结，与p2的引入顺序略有重叠。
issues.fix: 封面保留「两种每周阅读安排」和「本材料只记录讨论意见」的范围说明，把「没有测量阅读量或学习效果」的完整表述留给p5。

packets.title: Recorded net balances, 2021–2024: three values, unequal gaps, no measured cause

outline.heading: Recorded net balances, 2021–2024: three values, unequal gaps, no measured cause
outline.goal: State the core message up front: three recorded values, unequal spacing, no measured cause.
outline.message: The record contains exactly three synthetic net balances in units — -8 (2021), 4 (2022) and 12 (2024) — spaced one year then two years apart, and it does not identify what caused the changes.
outline.question: What does the recorded series actually say, and what does it leave open?

outline.heading: The recorded balance goes from -8 to 12 units, and all three values must be read as recorded
outline.goal: Show the three recorded values with their units and keep the negative value visible.
outline.link: first evidence: the recorded values themselves
outline.message: Observation: the recorded net balances are -8 units in 2021, 4 units in 2022 and 12 units in 2024; the negative value is part of the record, not an error to be dropped.
outline.question: Which values were actually recorded, and in what units?

outline.heading: The gaps between records are unequal: one year, then two
outline.goal: Make the unequal year intervals explicit so students do not assume an even spacing.
outline.link: addition: the spacing of the values just shown
outline.message: Observation: 2021 to 2022 is a one-year interval and 2022 to 2024 is a two-year interval; the record contains no 2023 value, so the spacing between points cannot be treated as uniform.
outline.question: How much time separates the records, and is that spacing even?

outline.heading: The records show values, not reasons
outline.goal: Separate the recorded values from any causal explanation, which was not measured.
outline.link: limit: what the recorded values cannot tell us
outline.message: The record reports year and net balance; it does not identify a cause for the change from -8 to 4 to 12 units. Any cause would be an interpretation added outside the evidence, not a finding of the record.
outline.question: Do the records explain why the balance changed?

outline.heading: Three observations are not a forecast, and a straight segment adds no 2023 value
outline.goal: Explain why the three points support neither a 2023 estimate nor a constant annual rate.
outline.link: further limit: the points do not predict or interpolate
outline.message: Limitation: the three observations are not a forecast. Connecting them with a straight segment does not establish an intermediate observation (for example in 2023) or a constant annual rate.
outline.question: What can we not read from these three points?

outline.heading: Read the series as three records: values in units, unequal gaps, no stated cause
outline.goal: Close on how students should describe and not over-read the series.
queries: units and intervals in data description
outline.link: consequence: how to state the series after seeing its limits
outline.message: The defensible summary is: net balances of -8, 4 and 12 units in 2021, 2022 and 2024, with one-year then two-year intervals, no recorded cause and no forecast.
outline.question: What is the safe way to state this series in an assignment or exam answer?

issues.problem: Page 2 is a bar_chart over the years 2021, 2022 and 2024. A categorical bar axis puts the three years at equal widths, which visually contradicts the unequal spacing that page 3 argues for; the brief explicitly asks that unequal year intervals be preserved.
issues.fix: Use a layout whose horizontal axis reflects real time (timeline / scatter on a year axis), or keep the table with years as labels and annotate 'axis not to scale'.

issues.problem: The page-1 message already states the values, the one-year/two-year spacing and the absence of a cause, and page 6 repeats the same sentence almost verbatim; pages 2–4 therefore re-state what the opening has said. In a 6-page deck this is heavy repetition of the same reasoning.
issues.fix: Let page 1 be orientation plus the core answer in headline form only, and let pages 2–4 carry the detail (values, intervals, no cause); keep page 6 as the only full restatement.

issues.problem: 'the record contains no 2023 value' is an inference from the list of recorded years (2021, 2022, 2024), not a statement in the evidence cards; stated as a fact about the record it goes slightly beyond what was measured.
issues.fix: Phrase it as 'no 2023 value is reported' or '2023 does not appear among the recorded years', which is what the evidence supports.

issues.problem: 'The record reports year and net balance' asserts the full set of recorded variables; the evidence only shows that a net balance in units is attached to each of three years.
issues.fix: Say 'the record gives a net balance in units for each of three years' rather than claiming an inventory of recorded variables.

issues.problem: 'constant annual rate' is introduced as a term without any explanation; for a student audience this is an unexplained prerequisite that the deck never defines.
issues.fix: Add a one-line gloss (e.g. the same number of units added each year) or a concrete example before using the term.

issues.problem: The deck title 'Recorded net balances, 2021–2024' can read as a continuous four-year record, which works against the unequal-spacing point made on page 3.
issues.fix: Name the recorded years explicitly: 'Recorded net balances, 2021, 2022 and 2024'.

requirements.reason: Brief: 'Preserve negative values'; supported by card 1.

requirements.reason: Brief: 'Preserve ... units'; supported by card 1.

requirements.requirement: Show the unequal year intervals: one year from 2021 to 2022, two years from 2022 to 2024.
requirements.reason: Brief: 'Preserve ... unequal year intervals'; supported by cards 1 and 2.

requirements.requirement: State that no causal explanation was measured / the records do not identify what caused the changes.
requirements.reason: Brief: 'No causal explanation was measured'; supported by cards 1 and 3.

requirements.requirement: Keep the no-forecast / no-interpolation limit: the three observations do not establish a 2023 value or a constant annual rate.
requirements.reason: Card 4 is the only statement of this limit; it guards against over-reading the series once unequal intervals are shown.

requirements.requirement: Frame the explanation for students (how to state the series correctly), not just as a data dump.
requirements.reason: Brief and approach name students as audience and 'explain the available evidence and its limits'; page 6 is the only page written for that use.

outline.heading: The conditional review process
outline.goal: State the deck's core message and set up the teaching sequence.
outline.message: This deck teaches the documented review process: collect the application, check whether required information is complete, and read the outcomes as conditional alternatives rather than consecutive steps [1][4].
outline.question: What is the one message this deck will establish?

outline.heading: The documented order is collect first, then check completeness
outline.goal: Establish the pre-branch order so the condition is not confused with an outcome.
outline.link: opens the sequence before any branch is shown
outline.message: The procedure begins by collecting the application; only after collection does it check whether required information is complete. This establishes order before any branch is used [1].
outline.question: What happens before the process branches?

outline.heading: The branch condition is whether required information is complete
outline.goal: Explain the condition before showing any branch outcome.
outline.link: after the order is clear, isolates the condition that triggers the branch
outline.message: The procedure names one condition for branching: required information must be complete. It places this check after collection and does not specify completion times or who is responsible [1][5].
outline.question: What exactly is tested before the two paths are used?

outline.heading: Complete and incomplete information lead to alternative paths, not consecutive steps
outline.goal: Present the branch only after the condition has been explained, and prevent reading the outcomes as a sequence.
queries: conditional alternatives complete begin analysis incomplete request information
completeness branch analysis request missing information
review process conditional outcomes not sequence
outline.link: uses the condition just defined to select one of two alternatives
outline.message: If the required information is complete, the next step is to begin analysis; if it is incomplete, the next step is to request missing information. These are conditional alternatives selected by the same check, not a sequence in which one outcome follows the other [1][2][3][4].
outline.question: What follows the completeness check, and how should the two outcomes be read?

outline.heading: The procedure does not specify timing, rates or responsibility, and a request is not a rejection
outline.goal: Record the limits and correct the inference that a missing-information request equals rejection.
queries: review procedure completion times acceptance rates responsibility
outline.link: adds the limits that constrain how the branch outcomes may be interpreted
outline.message: The documented process leaves completion times, acceptance rates and the responsible role unspecified. Requesting missing information is one of two conditional alternatives, so it does not by itself establish that the application is rejected [4][5].
outline.question: What can and cannot be concluded from the procedure?

outline.heading: Remember the condition, not a sequence toward rejection
outline.goal: Consolidate the conditional structure and the limits without adding unsupported actions.
outline.link: closes by restating the branch condition and the limits established earlier
outline.message: Collect the application, check whether required information is complete, and then follow the matching alternative. The procedure does not establish completion times, acceptance rates, responsibility, or rejection from a missing-information request [1][2][3][4][5].
outline.question: What should a student retain about the process and its limits?

issues.problem: The page-3 message cites [1][2] for the claim that the procedure specifies neither timing nor who is responsible, but card 2 is about complete information leading to analysis. That evidence sits in card 5, which is already assigned to this page but not cited.
issues.fix: Change the citation to [1][5], or delete the limits sentence here and leave it to page 5, which already covers timing, rates and responsibility.

issues.problem: The message repeats the limits material that page 5 exists to deliver (unspecified timing, unspecified responsibility), so the same reasoning appears on two pages.
issues.fix: Keep page 3 focused on the branch condition only; if a caveat is needed, add a short note that the procedure does not say who performs the completeness check, and point forward to page 5.

issues.problem: The wording repeats 'the next step is to ...' for both outcomes. Even with the disclaimer that they are alternatives, this invites the sequential reading the brief forbids. Page 2's message already models clearer wording ('only after collection does it check').
issues.fix: Phrase both outcomes with parallel conditional wording (e.g. 'if complete → begin analysis; if incomplete → request missing information') and lay them out as sibling branches from the same check, not as two boxes in a row.

issues.problem: The message calls requesting missing information 'an alternative branch', but that framing rests on card 4 (the branches are alternatives), not on card 5. The page cites only [5].
issues.fix: Add card 4 (or 3) to the assigned cards and citations, or restrict the message to what card 5 states: the request is not itself a rejection.

issues.problem: The page uses 'required information' as though it were defined, but card 1 never states which information counts as required, and no page tells the student this. The student audience may assume the material defines it.
issues.fix: Add an explicit note that the procedure does not define what 'required information' covers, or say that the deck stays silent because the evidence does.

issues.problem: The cover message states the full core answer in one dense sentence, including the key result that pages 4 to 6 explain. The title page therefore both hooks and argues the case.
issues.fix: Shorten the cover statement to the process and its conditional nature, and leave the detail on pages 4 and 6.

issues.problem: The closing message restates pages 2, 4 and 5 almost verbatim, so the takeaways add repetition rather than consolidation.
issues.fix: Frame page 6 as the two or three things a student should be able to do or say after the talk, and keep it to one short list.

requirements.reason: The brief states this explicitly; the proposed outline has six pages.

requirements.requirement: The branch condition must be explained on an earlier page than the page that shows the two outcomes.
requirements.reason: The brief says to explain the condition before using the branch. The outline does this (page 3 before page 4) and must keep that order.

requirements.requirement: The two outcomes must be presented as conditional alternatives, never as consecutive steps.
requirements.reason: The brief forbids showing both outcomes as consecutive steps; card 4 supplies the alternatives framing.

requirements.requirement: State the documented limits: no completion times, acceptance rates or responsible role, and a missing-information request is not a rejection.
requirements.reason: Card 5 is scoped as a limitation or decision boundary, and a teaching deck that omits these boundaries would invite unsupported conclusions.

requirements.requirement: Use language and framing suitable for students, with each new term explained before it is used.
requirements.reason: The brief specifies a student audience; 'required information' and 'analysis' are terms the source does not define.

outline.goal: Frame the deck as a comparison of two synthetic records with different scopes, without ranking them or pooling them.
outline.message: Two synthetic studies report different changes — 12% in a supervised laboratory (study A) and 3% in field use (study B) — under different settings; their records do not support pooling, so they are presented side by side.

issues.problem: The cover message says the records are "compared rather than pooled," but p1 is assigned only cards 1 and 2. That no-pooling/compare-not-pool conclusion comes from cards 3 and 4, so the factual cover subtitle lacks supporting assignments for part of its message.
issues.fix: Add cards 3 and 4 to p1, or remove the "so they are compared rather than pooled" clause from the cover message.

issues.problem: Across the cover, p4, and the p6 summary, the records are called "studies" or "records" without the "synthetic" qualifier used in cards 1 and 2 and retained in the p2/p3 messages. Dropping that qualifier changes how readers weigh the evidence.
issues.fix: Keep "synthetic" at first mention and in the closing summary, or consistently label the two studies as synthetic wherever they are named.

issues.problem: The cover title shortens "supervised laboratory" to "lab." The supervision qualifier is central to study A's scope and is lost in the one-line title.
issues.fix: Use "supervised laboratory" (or "supervised lab") in the title or subtitle.

issues.problem: p4 repeats the 12%/3% comparison already made on p1–p3 and says only "separate scopes" without naming the scope contrast. The compare slide could carry the unique scope comparison rather than repeating the figures.
issues.fix: Use p4 to contrast the two scope statements: supervised laboratory / did not evaluate field use vs field use / did not use study A's laboratory supervision.

issues.problem: p6 combines an interpretive summary ("defensible reading") with an imperative recommendation ("Report both figures..."). The recommendation is an explicit proposal, not an evidence result.
issues.fix: Label the recommendation separately, e.g. "Recommended use," or keep the summary and recommendation on distinct lines.

outline.heading: Reading the training diagram
outline.goal: Introduce Figure 1 as an illustrative training diagram, naming its documented order and its missing measures.
outline.message: Figure 1 is an illustrative training diagram whose three labels — Collection, Review and Archive — are connected in that reading order, with no duration, volume or quality measures [1][3].
outline.question: What does Figure 1 show, and what does it leave out?

outline.heading: The diagram has three boxes — Collection, Review and Archive — in that documented order
outline.goal: Explain the diagram's labels and sequence before any discussion of extension.
outline.link: opens the diagram by naming its three boxes
outline.message: The diagram contains three labelled boxes, and Collection connects to Review, which connects to Archive [1].
outline.question: Which labels appear, and in what order?

outline.heading: The arrows indicate a specified order, not a measured causal effect
outline.goal: Separate the sequence shown by the arrows from a causal claim the diagram does not establish, and note that the original labels must stay readable.
outline.link: separates the order shown from a causal claim
outline.message: The arrows specify the order of the stages, not a measured causal effect; the image is the original source illustration and its labels should remain readable [1][2].
outline.question: Do the arrows prove that Collection causes Review and Archive?

outline.heading: The diagram supplies no duration, volume or quality measures
outline.goal: State the diagram's limits so students do not read time, throughput or performance into it.
queries: duration volume quality measures training diagram
outline.link: adds what the diagram leaves unmeasured
outline.message: The diagram gives no duration, volume or quality measures, so it cannot support claims about time, throughput or performance [1][3].
outline.question: What duration, volume or quality information is missing?

outline.heading: A hypothetical extension could add duration, volume and quality measures while keeping the three labels
outline.goal: Present an extension explicitly as a proposal inferred from the missing measures, not as documented content; the cited cards support only its premises.
queries: extension training diagram added measures proposal
adding metrics to a process diagram
outline.link: turns the missing measures into an explicitly hypothetical proposal
outline.message: Hypothetical proposal, not described in any material card: one could add duration, volume and quality measures to the three existing labels. The cards cited support only the premises — the diagram lacks such measures [3] and its labels should stay readable [2]; no card describes or evaluates such an extension.
outline.question: Could the diagram be extended, and what would that require?

outline.heading: Read the diagram as an order, not as evidence of effect or performance
outline.goal: Summarise the supported reading rule and preserve the diagram's labels and limits.
outline.link: returns to the reading rule supported by the diagram
outline.message: Students should read the diagram as a documented order only, keep its labels readable, and treat any measurement or causal extension as a separate proposal with no evidence shown here [1][2][3].
outline.question: What should a student take away from the diagram?

issues.problem: p5 assigns cards 1–3 to a specific extension — adding duration, volume and quality measures — but none of those cards proposes or describes such an extension; they only establish that the diagram lacks those measures and that labels should remain readable. The heading's 'adds' also states the extension more strongly than the message's 'could add.'
issues.fix: Mark the extension explicitly as a hypothetical proposal inferred from the missing measures, make the heading conditional (e.g. 'could add'), and do not cite cards as support for the extension itself.

issues.problem: p6 adds a rule that any measurement or causal extension is 'separate evidence not shown here'; the cards do not say that, and 'causal extension' mixes a claim type with a measurement type.
issues.fix: Rephrase as a limit on the diagram: the diagram itself provides no such measures and does not establish causation; any added claims would need their own support. Avoid the undefined 'causal extension.'

issues.problem: p2 is the page that presents Figure 1, but it assigns only card 1; C2 states the image is the original source illustration and its labels should remain readable. A 'flow' layout could replace the original with a redrawing and lose that constraint.
issues.fix: Assign C2 to p2 and specify that the original Figure 1, or a redrawing that keeps every label readable, is used.

issues.problem: p4's message cites [1][3], but the page assignment is only [3]; card 1 is not assigned to p4, so the citation is not traceable on that page.
issues.fix: Add card 1 to p4 or cite only [3].

issues.problem: p4 paraphrases the missing measures as 'time, throughput or performance' instead of the diagram's terms 'duration, volume, quality'; this shifts the preserved limits and introduces terms not in the source.
issues.fix: Keep the exact terms duration, volume and quality; if paraphrasing for students, show the original terms alongside.

issues.problem: The missing-measures limit is already stated in full on the cover subtitle (p1), is then the main point of p4, and returns on p6; p1 and p4 partly repeat the same message rather than p1 setting up and p4 developing the limit.
issues.fix: Use p1 to identify the diagram and its order, keep the detailed limits on p4, and reserve p6 for a compact summary.
